The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required. Adler emphasizes the tracking and auditing capability: confirming 100% coverage of locations needing a patch or change.

The one customer proof point Adler offered comes from an early-access user at Merkari, which he describes as a global trading service from Japan with hundreds of independent microservices in production.

The user was fixing a code injection issue on GitHub involving environment variables. He ran the product on two repositories where he already knew the problem existed, then let the agent explore the rest of the codebase. It found 80 more potential vulnerabilities — all in configuration files.

Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said.

The unresolved question is whether this audit-and-coverage guarantee holds up at the 90,000-repository scale Adler cites as the bank's requirement. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings.

Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The same tools that speed up our work and allow us to write more code faster than ever before are also creating the conditions under which these vast codebases that run our world are starting to break down."

This is not an anti-AI argument. It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

For the software industry, the stakes are concentrated: the same companies driving AI adoption — large enterprises with thousands of repositories — are the ones least equipped to absorb the output. Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

sources.title: AI coding agents need good software engineers
passages: Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.
In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer.
In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline.
That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?
It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software.

extraction.body: For the past year, Silicon Valley has been telling us that software development is on the verge of becoming a prompt-and-ship exercise. You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it. Sure, maybe you could keep a few token senior engineers around to bless the output…or maybe not. I mean, Google’s Sundar Pichai says 75% of its new code is now AI-generated and reviewed by engineers, up sharply from earlier levels. Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed. When people who helped build the tools used by millions start warning that those same tools can produce buggy, potentially dangerous software at industrial scale, it’s probably time to rethink some of the assumptions fueling the AI wave. The right answer isn’t “AI coding is bad.” That’s silly. AI coding is powerful in roughly the same way power tools are powerful. Nearly correct is still very wrong I've made a related argument about the real cost of “nearly correct” AI code. It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software. As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code. AI hasn’t eliminated the need for that hard work. But a final draft that’s only 80% right is a liability, so I have to coach and oversee the agents. The problem is abdication The dumbest version of the AI coding debate asks whether AI will replace developers. Instead, it rewards the person who can tell, quickly and accurately, whether the output fits the system, the security model, the performance envelope, the user need, and the organization’s standards. In other words, AI rewards experience; it rewards people who know what “good” looks like. This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous. Not because agents can’t be useful, but because responsibility doesn’t scale the way prompts do. But when a company starts celebrating dozens or hundreds of agents churning out pull requests, issues, tests, migrations, and fixes, the obvious question is: Who actually understands what’s happening? If the answer is “another agent,” I’m sorry but we’re back where we started. InfoWorld reported that GitHub has considered stronger filters and maintainer controls to stem the flood. It’s cheap to generate but expensive to review. In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer. This is why the “human in the loop” language, tired as it has become, still matters. A junior developer accepting generated code because it passes the first test doesn’t solve the problem. Nor does a senior developer “reviewing” a flood of agent-written pull requests at a speed that makes real review impossible. For developers, AI is strongest when it’s used for bounded tasks like generating tests or explaining unfamiliar code. For managers, the worst possible metric is “percentage of code generated by AI.” That’s like measuring a newsroom by the percentage of sentences drafted by autocomplete. The 2025 DORA report on the state of AI-assisted software development gets at this more usefully: AI tends to amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If you have strong tests, clear ownership, disciplined review, good observability, and fast rollback, AI can make you better. In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline. You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo. At scale, keeping a human in the loop has to be enforced by architecture, not good intentions. In practice this means baking guardrails into the systems agents touch, like identity, data governance, and observability. The genuinely interesting shift I see across the industry, and yes, where Oracle is placing its bet, is pushing more of those controls down into the data layer itself, so agents operate against governed enterprise data rather than as clever scripts holding the keys to production. That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

coreStoryFacts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.

facts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.
It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends.
The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required.
Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world.
He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it.

He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising.
By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code.
Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk.
The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says.

The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.
In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer.
In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline.
That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code. The public image of software as a startup-and-solo-founder industry, he argues, describes almost none of the real workforce. The systems these engineers maintain are unglamorous but critical: real-time transaction rejection at a bank, reimbursement-rate calculation for a dual-coverage insurance policyholder, warehouse scanning behind Amazon deliveries, Uber arrival estimates, radar-based flight-path adjustment, payroll issuance, office air conditioning running continuously. "The software that runs the world is not attractive. It is not new. It is not clean. This is how everything really works," Adler said. He frames the session explicitly as "a call to honor the people, the owners of these codebases" — the maintainers doing what he describes as "the thankless but fundamental work." The core tension Adler identifies is between generation speed and comprehension capacity. Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving. He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising. Adler calls this "simply impossible." Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code. They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding. His claim is that repository architecture documented in agents.md files "changes almost nothing" in practice. The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says. But there is a hard limit: "You can't search for something you literally can't see." Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist. He names the vendors he claims are not solving this: OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and "anyone else." His concession is that their agents are "so incredibly good at solving the small tasks that most developers face every day" that demand is growing faster than ever — which is precisely why the large-scale breakdown goes unnoticed. The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm. The point: when agents discover and create vulnerabilities at unprecedented rates, telling a bank to use a coding agent to fix them doesn't address the problem of mapping how 90,000 repositories interact across all products. Adler's prescription is a fundamental graph of the codebase — including search and accurate compiler output — sitting in front of the agent. His formulation: "Visibility is infrastructure." The claim is that if you conduct this analysis, you empower agents to make changes effectively across the whole system rather than within a single repository. He predicts the code volume only grows: "These huge code bases are not going anywhere. In fact, there will be even more code." He acknowledges that model quality keeps improving and that major vendors will eventually add such capabilities. The tension sits unresolved. The product is designed to let an owner of a massive codebase commit changes to hundreds or thousands of repositories simultaneously from a single prompt. The user was fixing a code injection issue on GitHub involving environment variables. He ran the product on two repositories where he already knew the problem existed, then let the agent explore the rest of the codebase. It found 80 more potential vulnerabilities — all in configuration files. Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings. Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review. Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge? Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

sources.title: AI coding agents need good software engineers
passages: Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed.
You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it.
This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous.

As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code.
You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo.
In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer.
In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline.
That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?
It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software.

extraction.body: For the past year, Silicon Valley has been telling us that software development is on the verge of becoming a prompt-and-ship exercise. You know, just describe what you want and let an AI coding agent build it. Sure, maybe you could keep a few token senior engineers around to bless the output…or maybe not. I mean, Google’s Sundar Pichai says 75% of its new code is now AI-generated and reviewed by engineers, up sharply from earlier levels. Well… The Wall Street Journal recently highlighted warnings from Mario Zechner and Armin Ronacher, two engineers behind core pieces of the popular OpenClaw AI agent, who argue that AI coding tools are flooding software with what they call “vibe slop.” Their complaint is that too many people are using AI to skip the parts of software development that actually matter: design, judgment, testing, ownership, and deep understanding of the system being changed. When people who helped build the tools used by millions start warning that those same tools can produce buggy, potentially dangerous software at industrial scale, it’s probably time to rethink some of the assumptions fueling the AI wave. The right answer isn’t “AI coding is bad.” That’s silly. AI coding is powerful in roughly the same way power tools are powerful. Nearly correct is still very wrong I've made a related argument about the real cost of “nearly correct” AI code. It’s important to realize that generating code has never been the hard part of software. As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code. AI hasn’t eliminated the need for that hard work. But a final draft that’s only 80% right is a liability, so I have to coach and oversee the agents. The problem is abdication The dumbest version of the AI coding debate asks whether AI will replace developers. Instead, it rewards the person who can tell, quickly and accurately, whether the output fits the system, the security model, the performance envelope, the user need, and the organization’s standards. In other words, AI rewards experience; it rewards people who know what “good” looks like. This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous. Not because agents can’t be useful, but because responsibility doesn’t scale the way prompts do. But when a company starts celebrating dozens or hundreds of agents churning out pull requests, issues, tests, migrations, and fixes, the obvious question is: Who actually understands what’s happening? If the answer is “another agent,” I’m sorry but we’re back where we started. InfoWorld reported that GitHub has considered stronger filters and maintainer controls to stem the flood. It’s cheap to generate but expensive to review. In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer. This is why the “human in the loop” language, tired as it has become, still matters. A junior developer accepting generated code because it passes the first test doesn’t solve the problem. Nor does a senior developer “reviewing” a flood of agent-written pull requests at a speed that makes real review impossible. For developers, AI is strongest when it’s used for bounded tasks like generating tests or explaining unfamiliar code. For managers, the worst possible metric is “percentage of code generated by AI.” That’s like measuring a newsroom by the percentage of sentences drafted by autocomplete. The 2025 DORA report on the state of AI-assisted software development gets at this more usefully: AI tends to amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If you have strong tests, clear ownership, disciplined review, good observability, and fast rollback, AI can make you better. In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline. You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo. At scale, keeping a human in the loop has to be enforced by architecture, not good intentions. In practice this means baking guardrails into the systems agents touch, like identity, data governance, and observability. The genuinely interesting shift I see across the industry, and yes, where Oracle is placing its bet, is pushing more of those controls down into the data layer itself, so agents operate against governed enterprise data rather than as clever scripts holding the keys to production. That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

sources.title: Super Micro Contractor Pleads Guilty in $2.5 Billion AI Server Smuggling Case - Yahoo Finance
passages: Super Micro Computer ( SMCI:NASDAQ ) is back in an export-control headline after Reuters reported that a contractor tied to the company pleaded guilty in a scheme to smuggle servers packed with Nvidia AI chips into China , October 9.

Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, ‌including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. The United States and China are competing for dominance in AI, with both investing billions of dollars in a ‌technology seen ​as critical to economic growth, national security and military ⁠capabilities. In March, prosecutors charged Sun ⁠and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. The scheme began around October 2023, with Sun ​and others conspiring to export servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licenses, according to the indictment. Asked for ⁠comment on the guilty plea, California-based Super Micro ⁠referred to its prior statements that the company was not ​named as a defendant in the indictment and that it had no impact on its ​business operations. Super Micro terminated Sun and cut ties with the ‌other defendants earlier this year. Also indicted were the co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, who was a sales manager at Super Micro’s Taiwan office, while Sun was a contractor. A lawyer for Liaw – who co-founded Super Micro in ⁠1993 and joined its board in 2023 – did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chang’s lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment. The indictment described Sun as ⁠a broker and “fixer” who facilitated ‌orders and took steps to conceal the scheme. extraction.body: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges arising from a Nvidia chip smuggling case that prosecutors say diverted advanced US technology to China. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported . The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment. Sun admitted to four charges: conspiracy to violate US export controls, conspiracy to smuggle goods, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and obstruction of justice, Reuters reported, citing a court filing. Prosecutors first charged Sun in March 2026 alongside two others connected to Super Micro, including company co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, over the alleged diversion, according to the Department of Justice . The indictment accused the three of conspiring to route high-performance servers containing US AI technology to China beginning around 2024, without the required export licences. Court filings allege the group used fabricated documents and staged bogus equipment during a Commerce Department inspection to conceal that servers had already shipped to China, Reuters reported. The FBI’s Assistant Director in Charge, James C. Barnacle Jr., said the defendants used a pass-through company to hide their client list and conduct, according to an Associated Press account carried by Barchart . Prosecutors allege more than $510m of servers moved to Chinese customers in a single three-week window between late April and mid-May 2025, part of the wider $2.5bn scheme, Cryptopolitan reported . Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported. The distinction matters: Liaw, the co-defendant with the closest ties to the company, co-founded Super Micro and sat on its board before his March arrest in California, when he was released on bail. Liaw has pleaded not guilty and faces trial on 2 November 2026 in Manhattan federal court, meaning Sun’s admission is the first guilty plea among the three defendants, Startup Fortune reported . Chang remains at large. The timing — a guilty plea weeks before a co-defendant’s trial — typically signals cooperation with prosecutors, though neither Sun’s plea agreement nor any cooperation terms have been made public. The case has a cross-border dimension. Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes . The March indictment hit Super Micro shares hard: the stock fell about 33% the day the charges became public, according to CNBC . This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move. Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15. The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion. The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC . The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone. Attention now turns to Liaw’s trial date of 2 November, where prosecutors are expected to draw on evidence built around Sun’s admissions. A sentencing date for Sun has not been disclosed. Whether Super Micro faces any separate regulatory scrutiny tied to the export-control allegations, beyond the criminal case against individuals, remains an open question for investors tracking the company’s compliance disclosures. The case has a cross-border dimension. Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes .

The March indictment hit Super Micro shares hard: the stock fell about 33% the day the charges became public, according to CNBC . This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move. Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15.

The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion. The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC . The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone.

Attention now turns to Liaw’s trial date of 2 November, where prosecutors are expected to draw on evidence built around Sun’s admissions. A sentencing date for Sun has not been disclosed. Whether Super Micro faces any separate regulatory scrutiny tied to the export-control allegations, beyond the criminal case against individuals, remains an open question for investors tracking the company’s compliance disclosures.

passages: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges arising from a Nvidia chip smuggling case that prosecutors say diverted advanced US technology to China.
Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported .
The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion.
The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC .
The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone.

Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes .
This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move.
Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15.
Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported.
The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment.
Court filings allege the group used fabricated documents and staged bogus equipment during a Commerce Department inspection to conceal that servers had already shipped to China, Reuters reported.

extraction.body: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges arising from a Nvidia chip smuggling case that prosecutors say diverted advanced US technology to China. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported . The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment. Sun admitted to four charges: conspiracy to violate US export controls, conspiracy to smuggle goods, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and obstruction of justice, Reuters reported, citing a court filing. Prosecutors first charged Sun in March 2026 alongside two others connected to Super Micro, including company co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, over the alleged diversion, according to the Department of Justice . The indictment accused the three of conspiring to route high-performance servers containing US AI technology to China beginning around 2024, without the required export licences. Court filings allege the group used fabricated documents and staged bogus equipment during a Commerce Department inspection to conceal that servers had already shipped to China, Reuters reported. The FBI’s Assistant Director in Charge, James C. Barnacle Jr., said the defendants used a pass-through company to hide their client list and conduct, according to an Associated Press account carried by Barchart . Prosecutors allege more than $510m of servers moved to Chinese customers in a single three-week window between late April and mid-May 2025, part of the wider $2.5bn scheme, Cryptopolitan reported . Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported. The distinction matters: Liaw, the co-defendant with the closest ties to the company, co-founded Super Micro and sat on its board before his March arrest in California, when he was released on bail. Liaw has pleaded not guilty and faces trial on 2 November 2026 in Manhattan federal court, meaning Sun’s admission is the first guilty plea among the three defendants, Startup Fortune reported . Chang remains at large. The timing — a guilty plea weeks before a co-defendant’s trial — typically signals cooperation with prosecutors, though neither Sun’s plea agreement nor any cooperation terms have been made public. The case has a cross-border dimension. Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes . The March indictment hit Super Micro shares hard: the stock fell about 33% the day the charges became public, according to CNBC . This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move. Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15. The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion. The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC . The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone. Attention now turns to Liaw’s trial date of 2 November, where prosecutors are expected to draw on evidence built around Sun’s admissions. A sentencing date for Sun has not been disclosed. Whether Super Micro faces any separate regulatory scrutiny tied to the export-control allegations, beyond the criminal case against individuals, remains an open question for investors tracking the company’s compliance disclosures. Micron ( MU ) has agreed to settle a patent fight with Netlist , and the latter announced the deal on Tuesday.
Micron will pay $30 million per quarter for five years. That totals $600 million. In return, Micron gets a license to Netlist’s patent portfolio, including its “high bandwidth memory” technology.
The two companies have been in court for a while. In 2024, Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in a Texas federal court.
Then, in September, Netlist filed a new complaint at the US International Trade Commission. It asked for a ban on imports of Micron chips used in AI products from Google, Nvidia and Broadcom.
Netlist CEO C.K. Hong said the deal “further validates the value of our AI memory technologies.” Micron did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Netlist also settled a separate patent dispute with Samsung in August, after winning $421 million in verdicts against it.
See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Micron stock (It’s free) >>>
For Micron stock, the cost looks small. Micron made $33.2 billion in free cash flow in its latest quarter alone.
A $30 million quarterly payment is less than 0.1% of that. It also sits against $73.5 billion in cash and investments.
The bigger issue is risk. An import ban on chips used in AI products would have been a real problem.
Those chips are central to Micron’s growth. The sources provided do not say whether the new ITC complaint ends with this deal, so investors may want to watch for that detail.
The business itself is running hot. Micron’s latest quarter brought $54.2 billion in revenue and $33.42 in earnings per share.
Management expects about $61.5 billion in revenue next quarter. The company also says memory supply will stay tight through 2027 and 2028.
That is why this settlement matters less for the cash and more for the clarity. Micron stock has been driven by AI demand and strong pricing.
Removing a legal overhang lets investors focus on that story. Still, Micron stock now carries a recurring cost for five years, and investors will want to hear management’s view on it.

Here is why the market… Shares of Super Micro Computer ( NASDAQ:SMCI | SMCI Price Prediction ) are down 4% to $38.4 Monday morning, giving back part of last week’s rally as a fresh patent complaint over DDR5 memory modules lands on the AI server builders. The complaint names several major hardware vendors alongside memory supplier Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ). Dell Technologies ( NYSE:DELL ) stock is down 3% to $473.91 in midday trade. Hewlett Packard Enterprise ( NYSE:HPE ) shares are down 0.7% to $58.28, a much milder reaction than its two server peers. The Super Micro Computer stock move caps a huge run. The stock is still up 28% for the week and up 36% year to date, and well below its 52-week high of $58.68 set in October 2025. Netlist has filed a complaint at the International Trade Commission naming Super Micro Computer, Micron, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Lenovo over alleged infringement involving DDR5 memory module technology. The filing specifically targets DDR5 RDIMMs and MRDIMMs used in high-performance systems, the exact memory sitting at the heart of AI-optimized server platforms today. The complaint seeks an investigation plus potential exclusion and cease-and-desist orders covering the accused imported products. Netlist separately filed a federal lawsuit against Micron in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California involving two of the asserted patents. Dell Technologies was not named in the disclosed ITC complaint, which frames the Dell Technologies selloff as more of a sympathy trade than direct legal exposure. This is an allegation at the complaint stage with no finding of infringement, and any real business effect depends on the outcome, including a possible settlement. ITC investigations generally move on an expedited timetable compared with ordinary federal litigation, which is one reason server names are reacting even before an investigation has been formally instituted. Super Micro Computer’s fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $11.12 billion slightly missed estimates on short-term data center readiness delays. Adjusted EPS of $1.70 and adjusted EBITDA of $1.67 billion beat expectations, with gross margin jumping to 17.6%, a dramatic swing that reset how the market values the model. The company booked more than $60 billion in new orders during the quarter, pushing backlog to record levels, and management guided fiscal 2027 revenue of $65 billion to $72 billion. A cooler-than-expected July Producer Price Index reading added a macro tailwind late last week by reinforcing rate-cut expectations . Northland has flagged caution on the stock despite the strong results, which likely amplified the profit-taking impulse this morning. Micron stock is up 4% to $1,012.51 despite being named in the same Netlist filing. Micron shares are up 241% year to date, and today’s divergence from the server names supports reading today’s action as profit-taking plus legal overhang rather than a break in AI demand. The split reaction matters. Memory makers absorb component-level intellectual property (IP) disputes very differently from server original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) shipping finished systems that could face import restrictions if an ITC exclusion order eventually lands. That asymmetry is showing up cleanly in today’s prices, with the alleged infringer at the chip level rallying while its downstream customers fade. The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( NASDAQ:SOXX ) is up 2% to $563.23 and is up 83% year to date. The broader chip complex rallying while server builders slip supports reading Monday’s action as a rotation within AI hardware rather than a demand problem for the group. The iShares Semiconductor ETF is a broad semiconductor fund with meaningful sector-concentration risk, and it isn’t leveraged. Investors using SOXX for chip exposure may want to size their positions with that concentration in mind, particularly on days when idiosyncratic headlines split the group between memory and systems names. The suppliers underneath the AI buildout, power, cooling, networking, tend to trade on their own logic, and we profiled seven of them in a free report you can grab here . Investors can watch for whether the ITC institutes an investigation and on what timetable, and whether the parties settle before any exclusion decision. Traders may want to watch for signs the $60 billion Super Micro Computer order book converts on schedule through the September and December quarters. The near-term technical question is whether Super Micro Computer stock can hold its gains after a 28% week. A close back above Friday’s $39.84 level would take some of the sting out of the DDR5 headline, while further slippage could invite more profit-taking into the back half of the month. Ella Langley was forced to abruptly cancel tonight’s concert (Oct. 9) at BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of her Dandelion Tour due to a “serious security threat” involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist. Just a few hours before the show, BOK Center took to social media to announce the sudden cancellation in an “important show update,” explaining that the decision was made after careful consideration of the potential threat and the safety of everyone involved. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled,” the venue stated. The announcement continued, “The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.” BOK Center acknowledged the disappointment the cancellation would bring to concertgoers who had planned to attend the performance and apologized to fans affected by the decision. “The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first,” the venue added, noting that additional information and details regarding ticket refunds would be shared as soon as possible. Langley also addressed the cancellation, sharing a graphic of the BOK Center statement as well as her own, expressing her disappointment and apologizing to fans who had made plans to attend the show. According to the “ Choosin’ Texas ” singer, the decision was made following guidance from local authorities, the venue, and her security team. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team,” Langley’s statement on social media began. “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” Ella Langley is currently in the midst of her Dandelion Tour, which kicked off on May 7 at Huntington Center in Toledo, Ohio and continues through the end of October of 2026. The Dandelion Tour features support from Kameron Marlowe, Dylan Marlowe, Kaitlin Butts, Gabriella Rose, and Laci Kaye Booth on select dates. The trek comes in support of her latest album, Dandelion , which arrived on April 10 via SAWGOD Records/Columbia. Co-produced by Miranda Lambert and Ben West, Dandelion featured 18 tracks, including the project’s title track , “Be Her,” “Loving Life Again,” “Butterfly Season” and more, as well as the record-breaking, chart-topping hit “Choosin’ Texas.” Dandelion serves as the follow-up to her debut album, hungover , and marks Langley’s most personal album to date. “This record has so much growth in it. I’ve never poured more of myself into a project, into a song, into an idea, and it’s fallen out so beautifully. It’s about learning by yourself, making mistakes, and realizing that it’s all just part of life,” Langley previously shared in a statement. extraction.body: Country music is the lifeblood of Whiskey Riff, and we pride ourselves on standing firmly in the corner of the independent artists, and those few in the mainstream still doing it the right way. Whether it’s Waylon, Willie and legends of the past, or the superstars of today like Zach Bryan, our finger is always on the pulse of true country music. From Texas to Tennessee, Appalachia to Bakersfield, Whiskey Riff is THE unapologetic voice of the country music fan. A RIFF on what makes the great outdoors…great. “Country” is more than just a steel guitar. It’s a lifestyle, a mindset, and a way to speak your mind and not apologize for it. Whiskey Riff is that lifestyle. On ‘Whiskey Riff Raff’ buckle up for an unfiltered and unapologetic take on country music, life, sports, and all the craziness that comes with it. Laugh with us. Rant with us. Drink with us. This evening, Ella Langley was forced to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma slated for the BOK Center due to what is being described as “a serious security threat.” She says additional information, as well as refund information, will be shared as soon as possible: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled. The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concert and will always come first. Additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved.” Ella shared the news in a post on Instagram, saying she is very, very sorry for having to do this, noting that she knows “much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show.” We all know it takes a lot, so I’m sure fans will understandably be disappointed, but safety always comes first. She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” I know she would never do this so last minute if it wasn’t very serious, and while there’s no word on what the specific threat is, the priority is her safety and the safety of all fans, and that will always be the most important thing, and I’m sure she will be back to make it up to her fans when it’s safe to do so. As we near the end of the year, it’s becoming increasingly clear that 2026 will go down as the year of Ella Langley. Simply put, it’s hard to argue that she’s not just the hottest star in country music, but as music as a whole. If you’ve been paying close attention within the genre over the years, it was more than apparent that the Alabama native was bound to be a star, catching early buzz with tracks like “Country Boy’s Dream Girl,” “paint the town blue” and “That’s Why We Fight” with Koe Wetzel. With that being said, however, I don’t think anyone could have predicted the world-dominating, record-smashing success she’s had recently. Launching off the success of her Riley Green collaboration, “you look like you love me” throughout 2024 and 2025, as well as other hits such as “weren’t for the wind,” the Alabama native has become nothing short of a phenomenon thanks to the megahit that is “Choosin’ Texas,” And, in turn, she has captured the hearts of nearly everyone in the country and the world over the past year. Since its release on October 17th, it is now the longest-running #1 hit by a female artist this century, the only country song by a woman to triple up and go #1 on Billboard’s Hot 100, Hot Country and Country Airplay charts simultaneously. In case that wasn’t enough, thanks to the success of her sophomore album, Dandelion, which debuted at #1 on the all-genre Billboard 200 and sold 169,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. in its first week, Langley became just the second woman in history to hold the #1 album and song in the U.S. simultaneously with a country song/album. Two weeks ago, she made U.S. history by officially capturing the longest-running #1 hit in U.S. history with 23 weeks (now 24), passing Mariah Carey’s long-standing record of 22 atop the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, and her record year continues as she adds more certifications and records to her catalog.

Whether it’s Waylon, Willie and legends of the past, or the superstars of today like Zach Bryan, our finger is always on the pulse of true country music. From Texas to Tennessee, Appalachia to Bakersfield, Whiskey Riff is THE unapologetic voice of the country music fan. A RIFF on what makes the great outdoors…great. “Country” is more than just a steel guitar. It’s a lifestyle, a mindset, and a way to speak your mind and not apologize for it. Whiskey Riff is that lifestyle. On ‘Whiskey Riff Raff’ buckle up for an unfiltered and unapologetic take on country music, life, sports, and all the craziness that comes with it. Laugh with us. Rant with us. Drink with us. This evening, Ella Langley was forced to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma slated for the BOK Center due to what is being described as “a serious security threat.” She says additional information, as well as refund information, will be shared as soon as possible: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled. The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concert and will always come first. Additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved.” Ella shared the news in a post on Instagram, saying she is very, very sorry for having to do this, noting that she knows “much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show.” We all know it takes a lot, so I’m sure fans will understandably be disappointed, but safety always comes first. She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” I know she would never do this so last minute if it wasn’t very serious, and while there’s no word on what the specific threat is, the priority is her safety and the safety of all fans, and that will always be the most important thing, and I’m sure she will be back to make it up to her fans when it’s safe to do so. As we near the end of the year, it’s becoming increasingly clear that 2026 will go down as the year of Ella Langley. Simply put, it’s hard to argue that she’s not just the hottest star in country music, but as music as a whole. If you’ve been paying close attention within the genre over the years, it was more than apparent that the Alabama native was bound to be a star, catching early buzz with tracks like “Country Boy’s Dream Girl,” “paint the town blue” and “That’s Why We Fight” with Koe Wetzel. With that being said, however, I don’t think anyone could have predicted the world-dominating, record-smashing success she’s had recently. Launching off the success of her Riley Green collaboration, “you look like you love me” throughout 2024 and 2025, as well as other hits such as “weren’t for the wind,” the Alabama native has become nothing short of a phenomenon thanks to the megahit that is “Choosin’ Texas,” And, in turn, she has captured the hearts of nearly everyone in the country and the world over the past year. Since its release on October 17th, it is now the longest-running #1 hit by a female artist this century, the only country song by a woman to triple up and go #1 on Billboard’s Hot 100, Hot Country and Country Airplay charts simultaneously. In case that wasn’t enough, thanks to the success of her sophomore album, Dandelion, which debuted at #1 on the all-genre Billboard 200 and sold 169,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. in its first week, Langley became just the second woman in history to hold the #1 album and song in the U.S. simultaneously with a country song/album. Two weeks ago, she made U.S. history by officially capturing the longest-running #1 hit in U.S. history with 23 weeks (now 24), passing Mariah Carey’s long-standing record of 22 atop the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, and her record year continues as she adds more certifications and records to her catalog.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. sources.title: Margaret Hamilton, pioneering Apollo program software engineer, dies at 90
passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo. By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, the American computer scientist who led the development of software that helped NASA land astronauts on the Moon, has died at the age of 90, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced Wednesday.
Beyond her work at NASA, she published more than 130 papers and founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.
TWEET Reflecting on the Apollo program in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton recalled the responsibility carried by the young engineers developing the software.
Hamilton joined MIT in 1959, initially working in meteorology before moving into the Apollo project in 1965.
NASA, MIT pay tribute to computing pioneer NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman paid tribute to Hamilton on X, describing her as a pioneer whose work made humanity's first lunar journeys possible.
According to NASA, approximately three minutes before touchdown, her software intervened to overcome a faulty script, allowing the mission to continue safely.

Jerry Wohletz, CEO of Draper Laboratory, which emerged from MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory, said Hamilton's contributions to the Apollo Guidance Computer helped astronauts reach the lunar surface and return safely to Earth.

facts.text: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died.
In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.
And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.
Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959.
Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

“She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved," Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics told MIT News."Margaret Hamilton has been an inspiration to generations of computer scientists and engineers.

The trailblazing pioneer played a crucial role in the development of flight software for NASA's Apollo Program, which was responsible for taking humans to the moon for the first time. Hamilton was an integral part of NASA's Apollo program, which landed human beings on the moon for the first time in 1969.

Hamilton was given the medal by President Barack Obama in 2016. Obama said at the time, "Hamilton defined new forms of software engineering and helped launch an industry that would forever change human history.

Margaret Hamilton, the American computer scientist who led the development of software that helped NASA land astronauts on the Moon, has died at the age of 90, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced Wednesday.
Beyond her work at NASA, she published more than 130 papers and founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.
TWEET Reflecting on the Apollo program in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton recalled the responsibility carried by the young engineers developing the software.
Hamilton joined MIT in 1959, initially working in meteorology before moving into the Apollo project in 1965.
NASA, MIT pay tribute to computing pioneer NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman paid tribute to Hamilton on X, describing her as a pioneer whose work made humanity's first lunar journeys possible.
According to NASA, approximately three minutes before touchdown, her software intervened to overcome a faulty script, allowing the mission to continue safely.

Jerry Wohletz, CEO of Draper Laboratory, which emerged from MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory, said Hamilton's contributions to the Apollo Guidance Computer helped astronauts reach the lunar surface and return safely to Earth.
