extraction.body: Margaret Hamilton, a groundbreaking computer scientist who led the team that created the onboard flight software for NASA’s moon-bound Apollo program and later in life was celebrated as a powerful symbol of women in technology, has died. She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.” She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News. Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said. She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.” “She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.” Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death. Beyond her work at NASA, she published more than 130 papers and founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.

NASA, MIT pay tribute to computing pioneer NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman paid tribute to Hamilton on X, describing her as a pioneer whose work made humanity's first lunar journeys possible.
According to NASA, approximately three minutes before touchdown, her software intervened to overcome a faulty script, allowing the mission to continue safely.

Jerry Wohletz, CEO of Draper Laboratory, which emerged from MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory, said Hamilton's contributions to the Apollo Guidance Computer helped astronauts reach the lunar surface and return safely to Earth.

extraction.body: TULSA, Okla. — The BOK Center announced country music singer Ella Langley's Friday night concert has been canceled due to a "serious security threat." The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely either made by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. You can view the BOK Center's full statement below: The Tulsa Police Department released the following written and verbal statement addressing the situation: A sold-out concert was canceled tonight over threats of violence. Before the event, we swept the area with our K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol and BOK security for anything dangerous. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way." KTUL will provide more information as it becomes available.

extraction.body: Country music star Ella Langley canceled a scheduled performance at Tulsa's BOK Center, citing a serious security threat. The decision was taken just hours before the show on Friday night (local time). Langley, 27, announced the cancellation on Instagram, expressing her regret and emphasizing that fan safety is her top priority. Langley wrote, Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. She added, This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. Langley further said, I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can't tell you how sorry I am. According to local outlet News on 6, the concert was canceled due to a false bomb threat. The Tulsa Police Department stated that they found no credible threat after investigating the venue. They added that they had swept the area with their K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol, and BOK security for anything dangerous before the event. The BOK Center also confirmed the cancellation, stating that the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority. The incident is currently under investigation, and anyone with information has been asked to contact Tulsa Crime Stoppers.

The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely either made by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. You can view the BOK Center's full statement below: The Tulsa Police Department released the following written and verbal statement addressing the situation: A sold-out concert was canceled tonight over threats of violence. Before the event, we swept the area with our K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol and BOK security for anything dangerous. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way." KTUL will provide more information as it becomes available.

extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.

For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.

passages: TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, a new type of AI model that gained rapid popularity after launching just a few weeks ago, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.
The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Sequoia and existing investor DCVC.
The massive fundraise comes as little surprise given Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release .
The startup claims that a third of Fortune 500 companies are already using the model, a remarkably swift adoption by enterprises.
Jev is based on a transformer architecture, but it is not a large language model (LLM).

It doesn’t output text, but instead produces probabilities, or what the company calls “calibrated decisions.” What has users and large corporations so excited about Jev is TypeSafe’s claim that it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs.
The company positions its approach as uniquely suited for automating tasks rather than generating text or code.

The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models.
While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors.
But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat.

extraction.body: TypeSafe AI just closed an $870 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, valuing the startup at $7.5 billion just weeks after launching its groundbreaking non-text AI model Jev. The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models. TypeSafe AI just pulled off one of the year's most dramatic funding rounds, raising $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation mere weeks after unveiling Jev, its revolutionary non-text AI model. While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors. The non-text approach represents a fundamental departure from the language model arms race that's dominated AI funding, potentially opening entirely new categories of machine intelligence. [Embedded image: TypeSafe AI team celebrating funding announcement] The $7.5 billion valuation puts TypeSafe in rarified air. For context, Cognition recently hit a $48 billion valuation in the AI coding space, while other specialized AI startups have struggled to break the billion-dollar barrier. The speed of TypeSafe's ascent suggests Jev addresses a critical gap in current AI capabilities. What makes Jev different isn't just its non-text focus - it's the potential applications. While traditional large language models excel at text generation and analysis, they hit walls when dealing with other data types. The funding landscape for AI infrastructure has been brutal lately. Rising bond yields have hammered AI infrastructure funding, making debt-heavy data center buildouts prohibitively expensive. But TypeSafe's equity raise suggests investors see Jev as fundamentally different - a software breakthrough rather than a capital-intensive infrastructure play. The firm's bet on TypeSafe signals confidence that non-text AI represents the next major platform shift, potentially as significant as the move from rule-based systems to neural networks. OpenAI's recent DevDay showcased new Dots agents, but those still rely fundamentally on language model architectures. If Jev proves superior for non-text tasks, it could force a wholesale rethinking of AI development strategies across the industry. The secrecy around Jev's technical details mirrors the broader trend of world model AI startups going dark despite massive funding. But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat. Most companies have barely begun integrating text-based AI into their workflows. If non-text models like Jev prove more versatile for real-world applications - think manufacturing sensors, medical imaging, or autonomous systems - it could leapfrog the current generation of AI deployments entirely. The $870 million war chest gives TypeSafe serious runway to prove Jev's capabilities at scale. Unlike hardware-intensive AI companies that burn through funding on GPU clusters, software-focused approaches like TypeSafe's can stretch capital further while iterating rapidly on core algorithms. TypeSafe's meteoric rise from launch to $7.5 billion valuation in weeks represents more than just another AI funding milestone - it signals a potential paradigm shift toward specialized, non-text AI architectures. With Andreessen Horowitz's backing and $870 million in fresh capital, the company now faces the challenge of proving that Jev can deliver on its revolutionary promise. For an industry still grappling with the limits of language models, TypeSafe's success or failure could determine whether the next wave of AI breakthroughs comes from scaling existing approaches or fundamentally reimagining how machines process information.

extraction.body: TypeSafe AI just closed an $870 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, valuing the startup at $7.5 billion just weeks after launching its groundbreaking non-text AI model Jev. The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models. TypeSafe AI just pulled off one of the year's most dramatic funding rounds, raising $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation mere weeks after unveiling Jev, its revolutionary non-text AI model. While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors. The non-text approach represents a fundamental departure from the language model arms race that's dominated AI funding, potentially opening entirely new categories of machine intelligence. [Embedded image: TypeSafe AI team celebrating funding announcement] The $7.5 billion valuation puts TypeSafe in rarified air. For context, Cognition recently hit a $48 billion valuation in the AI coding space, while other specialized AI startups have struggled to break the billion-dollar barrier. The speed of TypeSafe's ascent suggests Jev addresses a critical gap in current AI capabilities. What makes Jev different isn't just its non-text focus - it's the potential applications. While traditional large language models excel at text generation and analysis, they hit walls when dealing with other data types. The funding landscape for AI infrastructure has been brutal lately. Rising bond yields have hammered AI infrastructure funding, making debt-heavy data center buildouts prohibitively expensive. But TypeSafe's equity raise suggests investors see Jev as fundamentally different - a software breakthrough rather than a capital-intensive infrastructure play. The firm's bet on TypeSafe signals confidence that non-text AI represents the next major platform shift, potentially as significant as the move from rule-based systems to neural networks. OpenAI's recent DevDay showcased new Dots agents, but those still rely fundamentally on language model architectures. If Jev proves superior for non-text tasks, it could force a wholesale rethinking of AI development strategies across the industry. The secrecy around Jev's technical details mirrors the broader trend of world model AI startups going dark despite massive funding. But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat. Most companies have barely begun integrating text-based AI into their workflows. If non-text models like Jev prove more versatile for real-world applications - think manufacturing sensors, medical imaging, or autonomous systems - it could leapfrog the current generation of AI deployments entirely. The $870 million war chest gives TypeSafe serious runway to prove Jev's capabilities at scale. Unlike hardware-intensive AI companies that burn through funding on GPU clusters, software-focused approaches like TypeSafe's can stretch capital further while iterating rapidly on core algorithms. TypeSafe's meteoric rise from launch to $7.5 billion valuation in weeks represents more than just another AI funding milestone - it signals a potential paradigm shift toward specialized, non-text AI architectures. With Andreessen Horowitz's backing and $870 million in fresh capital, the company now faces the challenge of proving that Jev can deliver on its revolutionary promise. For an industry still grappling with the limits of language models, TypeSafe's success or failure could determine whether the next wave of AI breakthroughs comes from scaling existing approaches or fundamentally reimagining how machines process information.

extraction.body: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor. Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago. Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees. Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market. “I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks. "“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck. “It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco. Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago. I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed. To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects. The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV.

Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds.
The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.
That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted.
It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.

"“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup.
Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete.
They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck.
The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said.
At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range.
The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture.

The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house.
According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management.
Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing.
From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest.
With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.

Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify.

Rivian was the blueprint, but now Slate and Telo have each shown off radically different takes on the truck of the future. America’s car dad Jay Leno has driven the Telo MT1 prototype on a new episode of Jay Leno’s Garage , and the video’s given us some interesting extra tidbits of information about this Mini Cooper-sized crew cab pickup. To start, the truck uses off-the-shelf 2170 cells, the same size found in the Tesla Model 3, but Telo plans on building the 106 kWh battery packs in-house. It all should add up to a targeted curb weight of 4,400 pounds, which is pretty light for any crew cab truck. That’s less than what a Toyota Tacoma TRD Off Road weighs, and that thing’s still powered by combustion. Interestingly, Telo claims to have taken advice from the first Tesla-certified body shop in America on ways to reduce collision repair costs, such as tie rod placement. Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles, and the steering column will change for production as the makers of the truck aren’t quite happy with the tilt range. Interestingly, the Telo is homologated as an MPV, opening the door for future body styles, but a crew cab truck is it for now. It’s very cab-forward but it isn’t cab-over, as a look inside with the door open reveals that the driver sort-of goes around the wheel well. Speaking of construction, Telo claims that production body panels for the first 5,000 vehicles will be stamped using low-cost Kirksite tooling, a cast aluminum and zinc alloy that requires very little finishing to create an accurate die, but is mainly geared toward small-batch production. As for the bed, it measures 62 inches long with the divider up, 48 inches wide between the wheel wells, “about 60 inches” above the wheel wells. However, drop the rear seats, fold down the partition between the bed and the cab, and Telo claims you’ll be able to load a sheet of plywood flat with the tailgate up. While we’re back there, the Telo features a NACS port behind the tail light, and the release to access the charging port seems like it’s going to be mechanical, with a latch replacing the magnets holding the flap closed on the prototype. Oh, and we need to talk about the Rivian-style tunnel under the bed, because Telo has big plans for it. The company eventually wants to build a three-row SUV-style configuration on this platform, and use the tunnel as the footwell for third-row occupants. Leno’s actually taken the Telo MT1 prototype out for a spin, which is a pretty good basis on whether a vehicle from a new firm is real or not—if someone not employed by the company has driven the vehicle on public roads, there’s a good chance there’s something behind the effort that’s more than hype.This is a pre-production model built by Aria Group in California so it’s definitely not a finished product, but this early glimpse seems a bit noisy on the public roads. There’s plenty of motor noise audible in the video, and you can hear a few rattles, although those vibrations will probably be sorted by production. Speaking of production, it seems that Telo has modest plans for its sub-$50k truck. As Chief Technology Officer Forrest North told Leno, “We’re not trying to have aspirations of going high-volume manufacturing out of the gates. We want to build small-batch vehicles, small numbers, get them in customers’ hands, scale from there.” Perhaps that modest goal is why, unlike many EV startups, the production timeline for the first customer Telo MT1s has shifted up from 2026 to late 2025. The plan is to build these trucks in America, likely in California to start, so we’ll be watching closely to see where this goes. Sorry, as logical as it is to ditch the classic 3 box truck shape, I can’t get behind the looks. All I see is the black rain frog from the shaved balls meme. They have contract manufacturing in California with a company that mainly does carbon fiber and manufacturing for airplanes. It sounds like that will be the first 5000 after that it sounds like they will be working in the Midwest I wonder if Foxconn? They haven’t really said if they will build their own factory all they said is they will always build their own packs. I think they are on the right track. Just moving to a real series production outside of California will reduce the cost a lot. They look like they want to exist around where Toyota does not cheap but not luxury or super premium. The one guy always talks about his Tacoma and kei trucks is where they got inspiration but they also talked to just about everyone they could on how to make something useable and fixable. Very smart and something you don’t see anymore. I think they have a winner and they aren’t in a rush which means they can probably make it. Agreed on all points M SV. 🙂 Plus, he has a giant dog, which always makes a person seem more sincere (in my foolish mind). 😉 And apparently just had a kid. They both seem like engineers in the bay area prison soon to escape to a better life after they can get free of the VCs. I’m not sure why so many people think they are a scam. They have a contract manufacturer and are on their way. Though I agree with a lot of people that the exterior styling of the slate is better, this is still the vehicle that suits my lifestyle and what I’m looking for in a truck. The longer bed, the mid-gate, the better range, towing and payload specs–it’s just actually what I want. Whereas with the Slate, I’d have to be compromising on all of those. I put a deposit down on the Telo truck last year and the Slate hasn’t convinced me to ask for it back. Now if Toyota were to release an EREV truck….. I’d strongly suspect this was months out, JerryRigEverything had a video on the Telo a month or two ago, well before the Slate launch, and from what I understand, Jay Leno’s garage has a long lead time for production by youtube standards. It is awfully funny timing, but I do also thing the pricing between the two trucks has a wide enough delta as to not completely conflict, although there will be some overlap. I see the Slate as a cheap EV workhorse while the Telo can be more of a do-everything vehicle with more seats, flexibility, and range, but that comes at do-everything pricing. Eh this would be much more useful for non-fleet use. The cost is the question. “Sub-50k” isn’t that compelling. I’ve emailed with Jason (the Telo CEO) and when I put down my deposit, I mentioned that I’d be looking for the cheaper, work-truck version rather than the 500 horsepower, four wheel drive version that’s been making the rounds on Youtube (complete with a glass roof I also don’t want or need). He gave me the impression that a work truck version would be available eventually, and based on what he said to Leno, I think it’ll be in the area of $40K (or hopefully, a bit less). But like most automakers, they’ll probably release the full-zoot, higher-margin version(s) first. If we’re talking work or barebones versions I don’t see the value of a Telo if Slate can meet their target price. Well, even w/a smaller battery and only two wheel drive, the Slate will likely have a longer range, more powerful motor, higher payload/towing capacities than a Slate would, plus the ability to carry 4’x8′ sheets of building material with the bed door up. Whether that will be worth the extra $10-12.5K that a base Telo will probably cost above a Slate would be up to the individual buyer I guess. I’m not sure what decision I’d make when the time comes… I’d want to drive both and see how they feel in day-to-day use, because that’ll be more of a deciding factor (to me) than any single specific feature. PS: at it’s likely MSRP of $27,500., the Slate is maybe a little too basic for the price. The (theoretical, hasn’t been specified/priced yet) base Telo might be about $41,500, so about $14K more. No point in including tax credits that not all buyers can qualify for, plus they might not even exist by the time these EVs are for sale. The numbers you point out are very important. At 27k the slate isn’t all that impressive. Their battery is probably about $17k that’s their biggest issue in think. And it’s shorts sighted. The telo on the other hand isn’t designed to be a bottom feeder. The one guy is always talking about his Tacoma and kei trucks I think that’s where they designed it to live as a cross between being an American kei and a Tacoma. They talked to everyone they could too and came up with the design plus besides medium duty trucks their hasn’t been a cab over pickup in the us in decades I think they are different enough to live together. The old ranger and the Tacoma /t100 lived together with slightly different buyers these two could attract even more diverse buyers. Of course, if any low-mile T100s turn up, they cost a fortune on Bring A Trailer, but whenever I see one around town, even if it’s a half-million-mile beater, I can’t help but think “dayum, that’s just the right size for me!” 🙂 Yeah I would say best to get in with the old guys if you want one. I’ve known several people basically get given nice older low mile Toyotas and others trucks when the old guys decide they can’t drive anymore. In the south they often refer to the older rangers, Tacomas and t100s as “pawpaw trucks” because so many old guy bought them and refuse to give them up. The jacked-up tech bro talking about the car really turned me off. Especially when he tried to dismiss Jay’s point about distracted drivers killing more pedestrians than ever by blaming it on phones instead of the terrible touchscreens that keep your eyes off the road. That interior is just garbage. I don’t see why they have to charge $50,000 for an uglier electric Subaru Brat, especially when they cheaped out on the dash and just stuck a bunch of glowing phones where real controls should go. You are aware that the truck Leno drove is a prototype, right? I mean, they said so f few times. Lots of details, including the interior bits, are still being ironed out. I don’t find it ugly at all, but would have preferred simple, round headlights, and have to imagine fitting some off-the-shelf LED round lamps would shave more than just a few dollars off of the cost. Well it looks vastly better than anything else for sale in the USA, and obviously has better visibility and safety in term of seeing what’s in front of you. But “A Mini Cooper-Sized Electric Truck” ?? What Mini cooper are we talking about here? The current one – a 2025 MINI Cooper 2-door Hatch/Hardtop is 152.6 inches long, the Telo is 152 inches even, so it is a half inch shorter than the smallest current MINI. This isn’t selling mainstream. I can design something better drunk. Sorry J I’m not really a truck person to begin with, but Telo pretty much ruins all other trucks for me, the packaging just seems so perfect and fit for purpose that everything else seems like a compromise (other than if you need to tow, of course, but you could do a lot of the same basic ideas with an ICE also, if you wanted to) Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles Yeah, the Slate is more cool, the Telo is more useful. Really depends if you go with your brain or your heart lol

extraction.body: Telo claims its upcoming electric pickup will be able to tow more than originally planned. According to the startup, the MT1 EV will have a higher towing capacity than a base Ford F-150. The 152-inch pickup will also out-tow the base Tesla Cybetruck. Telo, the California startup that's trying to bring a small but powerful electric pickup truck to the market, now wants to play with the big boys when it comes to towing. Forrest North, the company's cofounder and chief technology officer, said in a YouTube video posted on Friday that the upcoming MT1 four-door pickup will be able to tow up to 8,000 pounds, up from the previously planned 6,600 pounds. That's a big number for such a small vehicle. As a reminder, Telo's first vehicle, which is not being mass-produced yet, is just 152 inches long—the same as the latest-generation Mini two-door hatchback. Despite that, it has four doors, it can seat up to five people, and has a 60-inch bed in the back. And now, with the increased towing capacity, the Telo MT1 is shaping up to be quite the urban worker—small enough to fit on small city streets, yet powerful enough to do big jobs. "In that 8,000 pound range, it unlocks the ability to have some of the new trailers that are coming onto the market which have active regen and battery packs of their own," North said. The video shows the Telo towing one such electrified camper, the Pebble Flow , which has a 45-kilowatt-hour battery pack, two hub motors, and a gross weight of 6,800 lbs. The company says the small truck can comfortably tow up to the new limit thanks to the regenerative braking capabilities of its electric motors. The fact that the vehicle itself weighs 4,400 lbs also helps keep it planted on the road, North said. Its bespoke electric platform has enabled designers and engineers to place the axles as close as possible to the car's front and rear, making more room for the cabin. That also enables the Telo to handle more weight on the tow hitch, North said, since the short distance between the rear axle and the tow hitch results in less levering force that would impact the front end. When it comes to towing, the base 2026 Ford F-150 with the 2.7-liter V6 EcoBoost engine and standard axle ratio can carry between 7,400 and 7,600 pounds. Meanwhile, the much more expensive Tesla Cybertruck Dual-Motor is rated for 7,500 lbs, all of which puts the diminutive Telo MT1 in a better place than anyone could've expected. (Both the F-150 and Cybertruck are also available in versions that can tow 11,000 lbs or more.) Telo claims an estimated starting MSRP of $41,520 for the entry-level model with a single rear electric motor and 260 miles of range. That's about $2,000 more than the cheapest F-150, which only has two doors, and about $2,000 more expensive than the most affordable four-door F-150. It's also $30,000 less than the base Cybertruck , though it's worth noting that Telo's plans also include a $50,000 model with dual-motor all-wheel drive and 350 miles of estimated range. All of this sounds pretty good, but right now, nobody can experience what Telo is claiming, except for its own employees. The startup is still working on getting its funky urban pickup into production. It recently announced a manufacturing contract with Schwab Industries, a Tier 1 automotive supplier, which will build its body-in-whites . Telo says production is slated to begin at the end of this year. coreStoryFacts.text: The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

story.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body

facts.text: The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Rivian was the blueprint, but now Slate and Telo have each shown off radically different takes on the truck of the future.
He gave me the impression that a work truck version would be available eventually, and based on what he said to Leno, I think it’ll be in the area of $40K (or hopefully, a bit less).
Speaking of production, it seems that Telo has modest plans for its sub-$50k truck.
The current one – a 2025 MINI Cooper 2-door Hatch/Hardtop is 152.6 inches long, the Telo is 152 inches even, so it is a half inch shorter than the smallest current MINI.
To start, the truck uses off-the-shelf 2170 cells, the same size found in the Tesla Model 3, but Telo plans on building the 106 kWh battery packs in-house.
Interestingly, Telo claims to have taken advice from the first Tesla-certified body shop in America on ways to reduce collision repair costs, such as tie rod placement.

Well, even w/a smaller battery and only two wheel drive, the Slate will likely have a longer range, more powerful motor, higher payload/towing capacities than a Slate would, plus the ability to carry 4’x8′ sheets of building material with the bed door up.
You are aware that the truck Leno drove is a prototype, right?
I’ve known several people basically get given nice older low mile Toyotas and others trucks when the old guys decide they can’t drive anymore.
Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles
When it comes to towing, the base 2026 Ford F-150 with the 2.7-liter V6 EcoBoost engine and standard axle ratio can carry between 7,400 and 7,600 pounds.

Meanwhile, the much more expensive Tesla Cybertruck Dual-Motor is rated for 7,500 lbs, all of which puts the diminutive Telo MT1 in a better place than anyone could've expected. (Both the F-150 and Cybertruck are also available in versions that can tow 11,000 lbs or more.)
Telo claims an estimated starting MSRP of $41,520 for the entry-level model with a single rear electric motor and 260 miles of range.
The company says the small truck can comfortably tow up to the new limit thanks to the regenerative braking capabilities of its electric motors.
Telo says production is slated to begin at the end of this year.

extraction.body: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor. Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago. Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees. Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market. “I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks. "“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck. “It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco. Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago. I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed. To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects. The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify.

extraction.body: Telo claims its upcoming electric pickup will be able to tow more than originally planned. According to the startup, the MT1 EV will have a higher towing capacity than a base Ford F-150. The 152-inch pickup will also out-tow the base Tesla Cybetruck. Telo, the California startup that's trying to bring a small but powerful electric pickup truck to the market, now wants to play with the big boys when it comes to towing. Forrest North, the company's cofounder and chief technology officer, said in a YouTube video posted on Friday that the upcoming MT1 four-door pickup will be able to tow up to 8,000 pounds, up from the previously planned 6,600 pounds. That's a big number for such a small vehicle. As a reminder, Telo's first vehicle, which is not being mass-produced yet, is just 152 inches long—the same as the latest-generation Mini two-door hatchback. Despite that, it has four doors, it can seat up to five people, and has a 60-inch bed in the back. And now, with the increased towing capacity, the Telo MT1 is shaping up to be quite the urban worker—small enough to fit on small city streets, yet powerful enough to do big jobs. "In that 8,000 pound range, it unlocks the ability to have some of the new trailers that are coming onto the market which have active regen and battery packs of their own," North said. The video shows the Telo towing one such electrified camper, the Pebble Flow , which has a 45-kilowatt-hour battery pack, two hub motors, and a gross weight of 6,800 lbs. The company says the small truck can comfortably tow up to the new limit thanks to the regenerative braking capabilities of its electric motors. The fact that the vehicle itself weighs 4,400 lbs also helps keep it planted on the road, North said. Its bespoke electric platform has enabled designers and engineers to place the axles as close as possible to the car's front and rear, making more room for the cabin. That also enables the Telo to handle more weight on the tow hitch, North said, since the short distance between the rear axle and the tow hitch results in less levering force that would impact the front end. When it comes to towing, the base 2026 Ford F-150 with the 2.7-liter V6 EcoBoost engine and standard axle ratio can carry between 7,400 and 7,600 pounds. Meanwhile, the much more expensive Tesla Cybertruck Dual-Motor is rated for 7,500 lbs, all of which puts the diminutive Telo MT1 in a better place than anyone could've expected. (Both the F-150 and Cybertruck are also available in versions that can tow 11,000 lbs or more.) Telo claims an estimated starting MSRP of $41,520 for the entry-level model with a single rear electric motor and 260 miles of range. That's about $2,000 more than the cheapest F-150, which only has two doors, and about $2,000 more expensive than the most affordable four-door F-150. It's also $30,000 less than the base Cybertruck , though it's worth noting that Telo's plans also include a $50,000 model with dual-motor all-wheel drive and 350 miles of estimated range. All of this sounds pretty good, but right now, nobody can experience what Telo is claiming, except for its own employees. The startup is still working on getting its funky urban pickup into production. It recently announced a manufacturing contract with Schwab Industries, a Tier 1 automotive supplier, which will build its body-in-whites . Telo says production is slated to begin at the end of this year. That also enables the Telo to handle more weight on the tow hitch, North said, since the short distance between the rear axle and the tow hitch results in less levering force that would impact the front end.

When it comes to towing, the base 2026 Ford F-150 with the 2.7-liter V6 EcoBoost engine and standard axle ratio can carry between 7,400 and 7,600 pounds. Meanwhile, the much more expensive Tesla Cybertruck Dual-Motor is rated for 7,500 lbs, all of which puts the diminutive Telo MT1 in a better place than anyone could've expected. (Both the F-150 and Cybertruck are also available in versions that can tow 11,000 lbs or more.)

Telo claims an estimated starting MSRP of $41,520 for the entry-level model with a single rear electric motor and 260 miles of range. That's about $2,000 more than the cheapest F-150, which only has two doors, and about $2,000 more expensive than the most affordable four-door F-150. It's also $30,000 less than the base Cybertruck , though it's worth noting that Telo's plans also include a $50,000 model with dual-motor all-wheel drive and 350 miles of estimated range.

All of this sounds pretty good, but right now, nobody can experience what Telo is claiming, except for its own employees. The startup is still working on getting its funky urban pickup into production. It recently announced a manufacturing contract with Schwab Industries, a Tier 1 automotive supplier, which will build its body-in-whites . Telo says production is slated to begin at the end of this year.

"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made. BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and wellbeing of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. "We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend." sources.title: Cloudflare Absorbs Entire Deno Development Team, Consolidating Workers for Self-Hosted Operations - BigGo Finance
passages: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company.

The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure.

Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations.
At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud.
In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform.
Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months.
When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition.
Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced.

Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services.
In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in.

extraction.body: U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company. The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure. The announcement was posted on Cloudflare's official blog under the joint bylines of Dahl and the company's Kenton Varda. Deno published the same announcement on its own blog the same day. Neither company disclosed transaction terms, including any acquisition price. At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud. In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform. Going forward, the team will integrate celld with "workerd," the Workers runtime that Cloudflare has open-sourced, evolving it into a formally supported self-hosted solution. Dahl and Bert Belder will lead this effort. Dahl stated, "I'm joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model the mainstream way to build servers." Deno's leadership has decided to concentrate development resources on this shared foundation rather than continuing to operate an independent runtime and hosting service. With the integration, a phased wind-down plan has been outlined for Deno's existing products and services. Note: Timeline based on official announcements from both companies. Deno is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that Dahl unveiled in 2018, designed to address architectural shortcomings in Node.js with a more secure and modern approach. Dahl led Node.js's early development before leaving the project in 2012. In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in. His argument is straightforward: workerd is open source, and the code published is identical to what runs in Cloudflare's production environment. He noted there are actual cases of users migrating away from Workers using it. "Open-sourcing and providing an escape hatch is actually good business," Varda argued. He then identified the real challenge: workerd's Durable Objects only support a single instance and cannot scale. celld fills this gap, and it will be the core focus of the Deno team's work after joining. Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services. The answer that emerged was celld, a single binary written in Rust. celld's only external dependency is a single object storage bucket. It bakes all the fundamental elements of distributed processing—compute, relational database, queues, and WebSockets—directly into the programming model. In Dahl's words, "Scalability should be built into the programming model; each application shouldn't have to assemble its own infrastructure." The reason celld chose Cloudflare Workers' programming model as its foundation is the Durable Objects abstraction. Each Durable Object functions as a small, individually addressable server with an embedded SQLite database, runs single-threaded, and comes standard with synchronous access to a local database and WebSockets. Dahl sees this type of abstraction as particularly useful for agent harnesses—the execution substrate for AI agents—because it combines serverless execution, persistent state, WebSockets, and a high-level JavaScript interface all in one. Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months. When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition. Cloudflare pushed back, creating tension between the two parties. Additionally, late last year, Oven—the company behind the JavaScript runtime "Bun"—was acquired by AI company Anthropic, a similar development in the same space. The pattern of independent runtime developers being absorbed into larger platform companies continues. However, there are important differences between the Bun acquisition and Deno's integration. In Bun's case, Anthropic was seen as leveraging the runtime technology itself to strengthen its own AI infrastructure. In Deno's case, the primary focus is expanding the ecosystem of Cloudflare's existing Workers product. It is less an acquisition and more an integration of projects heading in the same direction. This announcement marks a major turning point for developers who have built applications on Deno. With official development of the Deno runtime ending after a one-year grace period, existing users will need to consider migration options. Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced. On the other hand, Deno's survival as an open-source project is guaranteed, leaving the door open for the community to fork and continue development. JSR will also continue operating, meaning part of the Deno ecosystem will live on atop Cloudflare's infrastructure. The JavaScript server-side world has seen multiple runtimes compete since Node.js debuted in 2009. Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations. The loss of yet another independent runtime option is a short-term blow for developers, but for the broader JavaScript server ecosystem, it may serve as a catalyst for wider adoption of a programming model that hides the complexity of distributed systems. Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations.
At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud.
In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform.
Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months.
When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition.
Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced.

Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services.
In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in.
