As Honeycomb Founder and CTO Charity Majors puts it, being a great software engineer “has far more to do with your ability to understand, maintain, explain, and manage a large body of software in production over time, as well as the ability to translate business needs into technical implementation” than to simply churn out lots of code. AI hasn’t eliminated the need for that hard work. But a final draft that’s only 80% right is a liability, so I have to coach and oversee the agents. The problem is abdication The dumbest version of the AI coding debate asks whether AI will replace developers. Instead, it rewards the person who can tell, quickly and accurately, whether the output fits the system, the security model, the performance envelope, the user need, and the organization’s standards. In other words, AI rewards experience; it rewards people who know what “good” looks like. This is why fleets of autonomous coding agents make me nervous. Not because agents can’t be useful, but because responsibility doesn’t scale the way prompts do. But when a company starts celebrating dozens or hundreds of agents churning out pull requests, issues, tests, migrations, and fixes, the obvious question is: Who actually understands what’s happening? If the answer is “another agent,” I’m sorry but we’re back where we started. InfoWorld reported that GitHub has considered stronger filters and maintainer controls to stem the flood. It’s cheap to generate but expensive to review. In his talk, “The Friction Is Your Judgment,” he and Cristina Poncela argue that agent-generated code has a way of drifting toward the locally convenient answer. This is why the “human in the loop” language, tired as it has become, still matters. A junior developer accepting generated code because it passes the first test doesn’t solve the problem. Nor does a senior developer “reviewing” a flood of agent-written pull requests at a speed that makes real review impossible. For developers, AI is strongest when it’s used for bounded tasks like generating tests or explaining unfamiliar code. For managers, the worst possible metric is “percentage of code generated by AI.” That’s like measuring a newsroom by the percentage of sentences drafted by autocomplete. The 2025 DORA report on the state of AI-assisted software development gets at this more usefully: AI tends to amplify an organization’s existing strengths and weaknesses. If you have strong tests, clear ownership, disciplined review, good observability, and fast rollback, AI can make you better. In other words, AI doesn’t eliminate the need for engineering discipline. You cannot make tens of thousands of engineers, analysts, marketers, lawyers, and salespeople reliably “slow down and check the work” through good intentions and a memo. At scale, keeping a human in the loop has to be enforced by architecture, not good intentions. In practice this means baking guardrails into the systems agents touch, like identity, data governance, and observability. The genuinely interesting shift I see across the industry, and yes, where Oracle is placing its bet, is pushing more of those controls down into the data layer itself, so agents operate against governed enterprise data rather than as clever scripts holding the keys to production. That’s not as exciting as saying agents will write all your code but guess what?

story.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software

facts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.
It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends.
The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required.
Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world.
He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it.

He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising.
By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code.
Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk.
The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says.

The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

extraction.body: NEW YORK, Oct 9 (Reuters) – A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer has pleaded guilty in a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips to China, a ​federal court filing showed on Friday. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, ‌including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Thursday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. The United States and China are competing for dominance in AI, with both investing billions of dollars in a ‌technology seen ​as critical to economic growth, national security and military ⁠capabilities. In March, prosecutors charged Sun ⁠and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws. The scheme began around October 2023, with Sun ​and others conspiring to export servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licenses, according to the indictment. Asked for ⁠comment on the guilty plea, California-based Super Micro ⁠referred to its prior statements that the company was not ​named as a defendant in the indictment and that it had no impact on its ​business operations. Super Micro terminated Sun and cut ties with the ‌other defendants earlier this year. Also indicted were the co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, who was a sales manager at Super Micro’s Taiwan office, while Sun was a contractor. A lawyer for Liaw – who co-founded Super Micro in ⁠1993 and joined its board in 2023 – did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chang’s lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment. The indictment described Sun as ⁠a broker and “fixer” who facilitated ‌orders and took steps to conceal the scheme. He ⁠helped stage “dummy” servers in December 2025 and made false statements ​to a ‌US Department of Commerce officer during an inspection of supposedly ​stored servers, ⁠which had already been diverted to China, according to the indictment. Washington has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia’s B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, were subject to the restrictions. (Reporting by Karen Freifeld in New York and Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil ​D’Silva and William Mallard)

Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported .
The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion.

The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone.

Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes .
This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move.
Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15.
Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported.
The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment.

extraction.body: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges arising from a Nvidia chip smuggling case that prosecutors say diverted advanced US technology to China. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported . The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment. Sun admitted to four charges: conspiracy to violate US export controls, conspiracy to smuggle goods, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and obstruction of justice, Reuters reported, citing a court filing. Prosecutors first charged Sun in March 2026 alongside two others connected to Super Micro, including company co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, over the alleged diversion, according to the Department of Justice . The indictment accused the three of conspiring to route high-performance servers containing US AI technology to China beginning around 2024, without the required export licences. Court filings allege the group used fabricated documents and staged bogus equipment during a Commerce Department inspection to conceal that servers had already shipped to China, Reuters reported. The FBI’s Assistant Director in Charge, James C. Barnacle Jr., said the defendants used a pass-through company to hide their client list and conduct, according to an Associated Press account carried by Barchart . Prosecutors allege more than $510m of servers moved to Chinese customers in a single three-week window between late April and mid-May 2025, part of the wider $2.5bn scheme, Cryptopolitan reported . Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported. The distinction matters: Liaw, the co-defendant with the closest ties to the company, co-founded Super Micro and sat on its board before his March arrest in California, when he was released on bail. Liaw has pleaded not guilty and faces trial on 2 November 2026 in Manhattan federal court, meaning Sun’s admission is the first guilty plea among the three defendants, Startup Fortune reported . Chang remains at large. The timing — a guilty plea weeks before a co-defendant’s trial — typically signals cooperation with prosecutors, though neither Sun’s plea agreement nor any cooperation terms have been made public. The case has a cross-border dimension. Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes . The March indictment hit Super Micro shares hard: the stock fell about 33% the day the charges became public, according to CNBC . This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move. Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15. The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion. The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC . The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone. Attention now turns to Liaw’s trial date of 2 November, where prosecutors are expected to draw on evidence built around Sun’s admissions. A sentencing date for Sun has not been disclosed. Whether Super Micro faces any separate regulatory scrutiny tied to the export-control allegations, beyond the criminal case against individuals, remains an open question for investors tracking the company’s compliance disclosures. extraction.body: A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ: SMCI) pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges arising from a Nvidia chip smuggling case that prosecutors say diverted advanced US technology to China. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun entered the plea in US District Court in Manhattan, Reuters reported . The alleged scheme involved diverting roughly $2.5bn worth of US AI servers fitted with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) chips to Chinese buyers, according to the original March 2026 indictment. Sun admitted to four charges: conspiracy to violate US export controls, conspiracy to smuggle goods, conspiracy to defraud the United States, and obstruction of justice, Reuters reported, citing a court filing. Prosecutors first charged Sun in March 2026 alongside two others connected to Super Micro, including company co-founder and former board member Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, over the alleged diversion, according to the Department of Justice . The indictment accused the three of conspiring to route high-performance servers containing US AI technology to China beginning around 2024, without the required export licences. Court filings allege the group used fabricated documents and staged bogus equipment during a Commerce Department inspection to conceal that servers had already shipped to China, Reuters reported. The FBI’s Assistant Director in Charge, James C. Barnacle Jr., said the defendants used a pass-through company to hide their client list and conduct, according to an Associated Press account carried by Barchart . Prosecutors allege more than $510m of servers moved to Chinese customers in a single three-week window between late April and mid-May 2025, part of the wider $2.5bn scheme, Cryptopolitan reported . Super Micro is not named as a defendant in the case, and the company has said the matter has not affected its operations, Reuters reported. The distinction matters: Liaw, the co-defendant with the closest ties to the company, co-founded Super Micro and sat on its board before his March arrest in California, when he was released on bail. Liaw has pleaded not guilty and faces trial on 2 November 2026 in Manhattan federal court, meaning Sun’s admission is the first guilty plea among the three defendants, Startup Fortune reported . Chang remains at large. The timing — a guilty plea weeks before a co-defendant’s trial — typically signals cooperation with prosecutors, though neither Sun’s plea agreement nor any cooperation terms have been made public. The case has a cross-border dimension. Taiwanese authorities separately detained several individuals, including Super Micro employees, in May and June 2026 as part of a related smuggling probe, two months after the US charges were unsealed, according to Forbes . The March indictment hit Super Micro shares hard: the stock fell about 33% the day the charges became public, according to CNBC . This week’s guilty plea produced no repeat of that move. Super Micro shares closed at $41.75 on 9 October, up 1.32% on the day, within a 20-day trading range of $40.025 to $45.15. The relatively contained reaction reflects the scale of Super Micro’s underlying business against the alleged diversion. The company reported revenue of $12.68bn and net income of $400.56m for its fiscal second quarter ended 31 December 2025, according to a 10-Q filed with the SEC . The $2.5bn alleged in the smuggling case represents a fraction of that quarterly turnover alone. Attention now turns to Liaw’s trial date of 2 November, where prosecutors are expected to draw on evidence built around Sun’s admissions. A sentencing date for Sun has not been disclosed. Whether Super Micro faces any separate regulatory scrutiny tied to the export-control allegations, beyond the criminal case against individuals, remains an open question for investors tracking the company’s compliance disclosures. The two companies have been in court for a while. In 2024, Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in a Texas federal court. Then, in September, Netlist filed a new complaint at the US International Trade Commission. It asked for a ban on imports of Micron chips used in AI products from Google, Nvidia and Broadcom. Netlist CEO C.K. Hong said the deal “further validates the value of our AI memory technologies.” Micron did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Netlist also settled a separate patent dispute with Samsung in August, after winning $421 million in verdicts against it. A $30 million quarterly payment is less than 0.1% of that. It also sits against $73.5 billion in cash and investments. The bigger issue is risk. An import ban on chips used in AI products would have been a real problem. Those chips are central to Micron’s growth. The sources provided do not say whether the new ITC complaint ends with this deal, so investors may want to watch for that detail. The business itself is running hot. Micron’s latest quarter brought $54.2 billion in revenue and $33.42 in earnings per share. Management expects about $61.5 billion in revenue next quarter. The company also says memory supply will stay tight through 2027 and 2028. That is why this settlement matters less for the cash and more for the clarity. Micron stock has been driven by AI demand and strong pricing. Removing a legal overhang lets investors focus on that story. Still, Micron stock now carries a recurring cost for five years, and investors will want to hear management’s view on it. extraction.body: @Baloncici from Getty Images via canva, @SUMALI IBNU CHAMID from Alemedia.id via Canva Now Live: Discover how much upside your favorite stocks could have using TIKR’s new Valuation Model (It’s free) >>> Micron ( MU ) has agreed to settle a patent fight with Netlist , and the latter announced the deal on Tuesday. Micron will pay $30 million per quarter for five years. That totals $600 million. In return, Micron gets a license to Netlist’s patent portfolio, including its “high bandwidth memory” technology. The two companies have been in court for a while. In 2024, Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in a Texas federal court. Then, in September, Netlist filed a new complaint at the US International Trade Commission. It asked for a ban on imports of Micron chips used in AI products from Google, Nvidia and Broadcom. Netlist CEO C.K. Hong said the deal “further validates the value of our AI memory technologies.” Micron did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Netlist also settled a separate patent dispute with Samsung in August, after winning $421 million in verdicts against it. See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Micron stock (It’s free) >>> For Micron stock, the cost looks small. Micron made $33.2 billion in free cash flow in its latest quarter alone. A $30 million quarterly payment is less than 0.1% of that. It also sits against $73.5 billion in cash and investments. The bigger issue is risk. An import ban on chips used in AI products would have been a real problem. Those chips are central to Micron’s growth. The sources provided do not say whether the new ITC complaint ends with this deal, so investors may want to watch for that detail. The business itself is running hot. Micron’s latest quarter brought $54.2 billion in revenue and $33.42 in earnings per share. Management expects about $61.5 billion in revenue next quarter. The company also says memory supply will stay tight through 2027 and 2028. That is why this settlement matters less for the cash and more for the clarity. Micron stock has been driven by AI demand and strong pricing. Removing a legal overhang lets investors focus on that story. Still, Micron stock now carries a recurring cost for five years, and investors will want to hear management’s view on it. The two companies have been in court for a while. In 2024, Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in a Texas federal court.
Then, in September, Netlist filed a new complaint at the US International Trade Commission. It asked for a ban on imports of Micron chips used in AI products from Google, Nvidia and Broadcom.
Netlist CEO C.K. Hong said the deal “further validates the value of our AI memory technologies.” Micron did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Netlist also settled a separate patent dispute with Samsung in August, after winning $421 million in verdicts against it.
See analysts’ growth forecasts and price targets for Micron stock (It’s free) >>>
For Micron stock, the cost looks small. Micron made $33.2 billion in free cash flow in its latest quarter alone.
A $30 million quarterly payment is less than 0.1% of that. It also sits against $73.5 billion in cash and investments.
The bigger issue is risk. An import ban on chips used in AI products would have been a real problem.
Those chips are central to Micron’s growth. The sources provided do not say whether the new ITC complaint ends with this deal, so investors may want to watch for that detail.
The business itself is running hot. Micron’s latest quarter brought $54.2 billion in revenue and $33.42 in earnings per share.
Management expects about $61.5 billion in revenue next quarter. The company also says memory supply will stay tight through 2027 and 2028.
That is why this settlement matters less for the cash and more for the clarity. Micron stock has been driven by AI demand and strong pricing.
Removing a legal overhang lets investors focus on that story. Still, Micron stock now carries a recurring cost for five years, and investors will want to hear management’s view on it.

In return, Micron gets a license to Netlist’s patent portfolio, including its “high bandwidth memory” technology.
In 2024, Netlist won a $445 million patent infringement verdict against Micron in a Texas federal court.
Netlist also settled a separate patent dispute with Samsung in August, after winning $421 million in verdicts against it.
Micron ( MU ) has agreed to settle a patent fight with Netlist , and the latter announced the deal on Tuesday.

Just a few hours before the show, BOK Center took to social media to announce the sudden cancellation in an “important show update,” explaining that the decision was made after careful consideration of the potential threat and the safety of everyone involved. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled,” the venue stated. The announcement continued, “The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.” BOK Center acknowledged the disappointment the cancellation would bring to concertgoers who had planned to attend the performance and apologized to fans affected by the decision. “The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first,” the venue added, noting that additional information and details regarding ticket refunds would be shared as soon as possible. Langley also addressed the cancellation, sharing a graphic of the BOK Center statement as well as her own, expressing her disappointment and apologizing to fans who had made plans to attend the show. According to the “ Choosin’ Texas ” singer, the decision was made following guidance from local authorities, the venue, and her security team. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team,” Langley’s statement on social media began. “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” Ella Langley is currently in the midst of her Dandelion Tour, which kicked off on May 7 at Huntington Center in Toledo, Ohio and continues through the end of October of 2026. The trek comes in support of her latest album, Dandelion , which arrived on April 10 via SAWGOD Records/Columbia. Co-produced by Miranda Lambert and Ben West, Dandelion featured 18 tracks, including the project’s title track , “Be Her,” “Loving Life Again,” “Butterfly Season” and more, as well as the record-breaking, chart-topping hit “Choosin’ Texas.” Dandelion serves as the follow-up to her debut album, hungover , and marks Langley’s most personal album to date. “This record has so much growth in it. I’ve never poured more of myself into a project, into a song, into an idea, and it’s fallen out so beautifully. extraction.body: Ella Langley revealed she made the difficult decision to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Okla., last minute due to serious security concerns: “I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” Ella Langley is putting the safety of her fans first. The country star, who is currently on her Dandelion Tour, canceled her Oct. 9 show at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Okla., just hours before taking the stage due to security concerns. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” Langley wrote in an Oct. 9 Instagram post. “This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.” The “Choosin’ Texas” singer emphasized that having to cancel the show was “not a decision that was made lightly.” “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am,” she continued. “I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” As for concertgoers who purchased tickets, the BOK Center noted in a separate statement that “additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible.” Langley kicked off her 38-stop tour in May to support her second album of the same name. The concert series will conclude at the end of October. While the “Be Her” artist didn’t address whether or not the Oct. 9 concert cancelation will impact further dates, she is scheduled to perform in Lubbock, Texas on Oct. 10, followed by stops in Los Angeles, Salt Lake City, Des Moines and Lincoln, before wrapping up her tour on Halloween in Saint Paul, Minn. Throughout her tour, the “You Look Like You Love Me” singer has been chronicling her experiences on social media. “Knoxville, Columbus & Moline,” Langley wrote alongside a carousel of concert photos in a Sept. 27 Instagram post. “Every single night of this tour is so special, I can’t thank y’all enough.” Your source for entertainment news, celebrities, celeb news, and ​celebrity gossip. passages: Ella Langley revealed she made the difficult decision to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Okla., last minute due to serious security concerns: “I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.”
Ella Langley is putting the safety of her fans first.
The country star, who is currently on her Dandelion Tour, canceled her Oct. 9 show at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Okla., just hours before taking the stage due to security concerns.

“Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” Langley wrote in an Oct. 9 Instagram post. “This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.”
The “Choosin’ Texas” singer emphasized that having to cancel the show was “not a decision that was made lightly.”

“I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am,” she continued. “I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.”
As for concertgoers who purchased tickets, the BOK Center noted in a separate statement that “additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible.”
Langley kicked off her 38-stop tour in May to support her second album of the same name. The concert series will conclude at the end of October.

While the “Be Her” artist didn’t address whether or not the Oct. 9 concert cancelation will impact further dates, she is scheduled to perform in Lubbock, Texas on Oct. 10, followed by stops in Los Angeles, Salt Lake City, Des Moines and Lincoln, before wrapping up her tour on Halloween in Saint Paul, Minn.
Throughout her tour, the “You Look Like You Love Me” singer has been chronicling her experiences on social media.
“Knoxville, Columbus & Moline,” Langley wrote alongside a carousel of concert photos in a Sept. 27 Instagram post. “Every single night of this tour is so special, I can’t thank y’all enough.”

This evening, Ella Langley was forced to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma slated for the BOK Center due to what is being described as “a serious security threat.” She says additional information, as well as refund information, will be shared as soon as possible: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled. The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concert and will always come first. Additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved.” Ella shared the news in a post on Instagram, saying she is very, very sorry for having to do this, noting that she knows “much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show.” We all know it takes a lot, so I’m sure fans will understandably be disappointed, but safety always comes first. She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” I know she would never do this so last minute if it wasn’t very serious, and while there’s no word on what the specific threat is, the priority is her safety and the safety of all fans, and that will always be the most important thing, and I’m sure she will be back to make it up to her fans when it’s safe to do so. As we near the end of the year, it’s becoming increasingly clear that 2026 will go down as the year of Ella Langley. Simply put, it’s hard to argue that she’s not just the hottest star in country music, but as music as a whole. If you’ve been paying close attention within the genre over the years, it was more than apparent that the Alabama native was bound to be a star, catching early buzz with tracks like “Country Boy’s Dream Girl,” “paint the town blue” and “That’s Why We Fight” with Koe Wetzel. With that being said, however, I don’t think anyone could have predicted the world-dominating, record-smashing success she’s had recently. Launching off the success of her Riley Green collaboration, “you look like you love me” throughout 2024 and 2025, as well as other hits such as “weren’t for the wind,” the Alabama native has become nothing short of a phenomenon thanks to the megahit that is “Choosin’ Texas,” And, in turn, she has captured the hearts of nearly everyone in the country and the world over the past year. Since its release on October 17th, it is now the longest-running #1 hit by a female artist this century, the only country song by a woman to triple up and go #1 on Billboard’s Hot 100, Hot Country and Country Airplay charts simultaneously. In case that wasn’t enough, thanks to the success of her sophomore album, Dandelion, which debuted at #1 on the all-genre Billboard 200 and sold 169,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. in its first week, Langley became just the second woman in history to hold the #1 album and song in the U.S. simultaneously with a country song/album. Two weeks ago, she made U.S. history by officially capturing the longest-running #1 hit in U.S. history with 23 weeks (now 24), passing Mariah Carey’s long-standing record of 22 atop the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, and her record year continues as she adds more certifications and records to her catalog.

She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team:

“Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.

I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. Langley also addressed the cancellation, sharing a graphic of the BOK Center statement as well as her own, expressing her disappointment and apologizing to fans who had made plans to attend the show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team,” Langley’s statement on social media began. “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project.
A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton.

Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article.
In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

She was 90. Hamilton died Sept. 30 at a hospital in Cambridge, Massachusetts, her daughter, Lauren Hamilton, told The Associated Press on Thursday. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News. “We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.” “Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely either made by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way." KTUL will provide more information as it becomes available.

extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. The average time from submitting a merge request to its integration into the codebase increased by 49% after AI agents were introduced. The share of requests in which reviewers required changes nearly doubled, while the number of comments per request rose by 35%.

In response, the share of employees involved in code review increased by 14%. At the same time, the researchers were unable to link AI use to significant changes in overall employment at these companies after comparing Jellyfish and LinkedIn data.

As of March 2026, 80% of companies in the sample used some AI tools for code review. However, AI agents left 23.3% of all comments during reviews and were responsible for 10.8% of all merge requests, so most of this work remained with humans. According to the authors, 95% of companies in the sample had already introduced AI agents for programming.

facts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

passages: TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, a new type of AI model that gained rapid popularity after launching just a few weeks ago, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation.
The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Sequoia and existing investor DCVC.
The massive fundraise comes as little surprise given Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release .
The startup claims that a third of Fortune 500 companies are already using the model, a remarkably swift adoption by enterprises.
Jev is based on a transformer architecture, but it is not a large language model (LLM).

It doesn’t output text, but instead produces probabilities, or what the company calls “calibrated decisions.” What has users and large corporations so excited about Jev is TypeSafe’s claim that it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs.
The company positions its approach as uniquely suited for automating tasks rather than generating text or code.

extraction.body: TypeSafe AI just closed an $870 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, valuing the startup at $7.5 billion just weeks after launching its groundbreaking non-text AI model Jev. The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models. TypeSafe AI just pulled off one of the year's most dramatic funding rounds, raising $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation mere weeks after unveiling Jev, its revolutionary non-text AI model. While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors. The non-text approach represents a fundamental departure from the language model arms race that's dominated AI funding, potentially opening entirely new categories of machine intelligence. [Embedded image: TypeSafe AI team celebrating funding announcement] The $7.5 billion valuation puts TypeSafe in rarified air. For context, Cognition recently hit a $48 billion valuation in the AI coding space, while other specialized AI startups have struggled to break the billion-dollar barrier. The speed of TypeSafe's ascent suggests Jev addresses a critical gap in current AI capabilities. What makes Jev different isn't just its non-text focus - it's the potential applications. While traditional large language models excel at text generation and analysis, they hit walls when dealing with other data types. The funding landscape for AI infrastructure has been brutal lately. Rising bond yields have hammered AI infrastructure funding, making debt-heavy data center buildouts prohibitively expensive. But TypeSafe's equity raise suggests investors see Jev as fundamentally different - a software breakthrough rather than a capital-intensive infrastructure play. The firm's bet on TypeSafe signals confidence that non-text AI represents the next major platform shift, potentially as significant as the move from rule-based systems to neural networks. OpenAI's recent DevDay showcased new Dots agents, but those still rely fundamentally on language model architectures. If Jev proves superior for non-text tasks, it could force a wholesale rethinking of AI development strategies across the industry. The secrecy around Jev's technical details mirrors the broader trend of world model AI startups going dark despite massive funding. But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat. Most companies have barely begun integrating text-based AI into their workflows. If non-text models like Jev prove more versatile for real-world applications - think manufacturing sensors, medical imaging, or autonomous systems - it could leapfrog the current generation of AI deployments entirely. The $870 million war chest gives TypeSafe serious runway to prove Jev's capabilities at scale. Unlike hardware-intensive AI companies that burn through funding on GPU clusters, software-focused approaches like TypeSafe's can stretch capital further while iterating rapidly on core algorithms. TypeSafe's meteoric rise from launch to $7.5 billion valuation in weeks represents more than just another AI funding milestone - it signals a potential paradigm shift toward specialized, non-text AI architectures. With Andreessen Horowitz's backing and $870 million in fresh capital, the company now faces the challenge of proving that Jev can deliver on its revolutionary promise. For an industry still grappling with the limits of language models, TypeSafe's success or failure could determine whether the next wave of AI breakthroughs comes from scaling existing approaches or fundamentally reimagining how machines process information.

extraction.body: TypeSafe AI just closed an $870 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz, valuing the startup at $7.5 billion just weeks after launching its groundbreaking non-text AI model Jev. The staggering valuation puts TypeSafe among the most valuable AI startups globally, signaling massive investor appetite for alternatives to traditional language models. TypeSafe AI just pulled off one of the year's most dramatic funding rounds, raising $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation mere weeks after unveiling Jev, its revolutionary non-text AI model. While most AI companies spend months or years proving their technology before commanding billion-dollar valuations, TypeSafe's Jev model appears to have struck an immediate chord with investors. The non-text approach represents a fundamental departure from the language model arms race that's dominated AI funding, potentially opening entirely new categories of machine intelligence. [Embedded image: TypeSafe AI team celebrating funding announcement] The $7.5 billion valuation puts TypeSafe in rarified air. For context, Cognition recently hit a $48 billion valuation in the AI coding space, while other specialized AI startups have struggled to break the billion-dollar barrier. The speed of TypeSafe's ascent suggests Jev addresses a critical gap in current AI capabilities. What makes Jev different isn't just its non-text focus - it's the potential applications. While traditional large language models excel at text generation and analysis, they hit walls when dealing with other data types. The funding landscape for AI infrastructure has been brutal lately. Rising bond yields have hammered AI infrastructure funding, making debt-heavy data center buildouts prohibitively expensive. But TypeSafe's equity raise suggests investors see Jev as fundamentally different - a software breakthrough rather than a capital-intensive infrastructure play. The firm's bet on TypeSafe signals confidence that non-text AI represents the next major platform shift, potentially as significant as the move from rule-based systems to neural networks. OpenAI's recent DevDay showcased new Dots agents, but those still rely fundamentally on language model architectures. If Jev proves superior for non-text tasks, it could force a wholesale rethinking of AI development strategies across the industry. The secrecy around Jev's technical details mirrors the broader trend of world model AI startups going dark despite massive funding. But TypeSafe's willingness to launch publicly, even with limited technical disclosure, suggests confidence in their competitive moat. Most companies have barely begun integrating text-based AI into their workflows. If non-text models like Jev prove more versatile for real-world applications - think manufacturing sensors, medical imaging, or autonomous systems - it could leapfrog the current generation of AI deployments entirely. The $870 million war chest gives TypeSafe serious runway to prove Jev's capabilities at scale. Unlike hardware-intensive AI companies that burn through funding on GPU clusters, software-focused approaches like TypeSafe's can stretch capital further while iterating rapidly on core algorithms. TypeSafe's meteoric rise from launch to $7.5 billion valuation in weeks represents more than just another AI funding milestone - it signals a potential paradigm shift toward specialized, non-text AI architectures. With Andreessen Horowitz's backing and $870 million in fresh capital, the company now faces the challenge of proving that Jev can deliver on its revolutionary promise. For an industry still grappling with the limits of language models, TypeSafe's success or failure could determine whether the next wave of AI breakthroughs comes from scaling existing approaches or fundamentally reimagining how machines process information.

extraction.body: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor. Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago. Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees. Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market. “I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks. "“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck. “It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco. Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago. I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed. Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify.
passages: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV.

Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds.
The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.
That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted.
It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.

"“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup.
Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete.
They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck.
The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said.

Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house.

Rivian was the blueprint, but now Slate and Telo have each shown off radically different takes on the truck of the future. America’s car dad Jay Leno has driven the Telo MT1 prototype on a new episode of Jay Leno’s Garage , and the video’s given us some interesting extra tidbits of information about this Mini Cooper-sized crew cab pickup. To start, the truck uses off-the-shelf 2170 cells, the same size found in the Tesla Model 3, but Telo plans on building the 106 kWh battery packs in-house. It all should add up to a targeted curb weight of 4,400 pounds, which is pretty light for any crew cab truck. That’s less than what a Toyota Tacoma TRD Off Road weighs, and that thing’s still powered by combustion. Interestingly, Telo claims to have taken advice from the first Tesla-certified body shop in America on ways to reduce collision repair costs, such as tie rod placement. Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles, and the steering column will change for production as the makers of the truck aren’t quite happy with the tilt range. Interestingly, the Telo is homologated as an MPV, opening the door for future body styles, but a crew cab truck is it for now. It’s very cab-forward but it isn’t cab-over, as a look inside with the door open reveals that the driver sort-of goes around the wheel well. Speaking of construction, Telo claims that production body panels for the first 5,000 vehicles will be stamped using low-cost Kirksite tooling, a cast aluminum and zinc alloy that requires very little finishing to create an accurate die, but is mainly geared toward small-batch production. As for the bed, it measures 62 inches long with the divider up, 48 inches wide between the wheel wells, “about 60 inches” above the wheel wells. However, drop the rear seats, fold down the partition between the bed and the cab, and Telo claims you’ll be able to load a sheet of plywood flat with the tailgate up. While we’re back there, the Telo features a NACS port behind the tail light, and the release to access the charging port seems like it’s going to be mechanical, with a latch replacing the magnets holding the flap closed on the prototype. Oh, and we need to talk about the Rivian-style tunnel under the bed, because Telo has big plans for it. The company eventually wants to build a three-row SUV-style configuration on this platform, and use the tunnel as the footwell for third-row occupants. Leno’s actually taken the Telo MT1 prototype out for a spin, which is a pretty good basis on whether a vehicle from a new firm is real or not—if someone not employed by the company has driven the vehicle on public roads, there’s a good chance there’s something behind the effort that’s more than hype.This is a pre-production model built by Aria Group in California so it’s definitely not a finished product, but this early glimpse seems a bit noisy on the public roads. There’s plenty of motor noise audible in the video, and you can hear a few rattles, although those vibrations will probably be sorted by production. Speaking of production, it seems that Telo has modest plans for its sub-$50k truck. As Chief Technology Officer Forrest North told Leno, “We’re not trying to have aspirations of going high-volume manufacturing out of the gates. We want to build small-batch vehicles, small numbers, get them in customers’ hands, scale from there.” Perhaps that modest goal is why, unlike many EV startups, the production timeline for the first customer Telo MT1s has shifted up from 2026 to late 2025. The plan is to build these trucks in America, likely in California to start, so we’ll be watching closely to see where this goes.
